Subject: Private GPU pool sizing — baseline throughput / burst question

Hi Karthik / Naomi,

Hope you’re doing well. Quick context: we’re moving the Cleo public chat assistant into our private VPC and want a concrete sizing recommendation for the initial GPU pool. Our current traffic profile (prod) is: typical steady requests ~65 RPS with median request length 140 tokens, peak bursts occasionally spiking to ~220 RPS for short windows (~3–7 minutes).

Goals:
- Keep 95th+ latency targets for first-token under 350ms for interactive flows.
- Avoid cold-start tail for KV/cache-heavy prompts.
- Capacity plan that supports sustained load for business hours and absorbs 2–3x short bursts.

Can you propose a sustained vs transient (burst) allocation, plus warmup and autoscale guidance? Also flagged: we need a network checklist for the private deployment (MTU/QoS/NAT sizing). Attaching our rough throughput numbers (we don’t have a formal model) — please advise if you want more telemetry.

Thanks,
Ben

Subject: Re: Private GPU pool sizing — baseline throughput / burst question

Ben — thanks for the profile, this is the right level of detail to start. I’ve sketched a pragmatic plan below (attaching a quick capacity model XLSX). TL;DR: size for sustained load + 50% headroom and reserve a modest transient buffer (either warm warm spare GPUs or short-lived burst nodes) to cover the 2–3x spikes.

High-level assumptions we used:
- Model: 70B-class transformer (quantized runtime) — typical token throughput per A100-80GB *shared* instance ~1500–2000 tokens/s depending on batch/kv cache behavior.
- Median tokens/request: 140 (your number) => sustained RPS target 65 -> ~9,100 tokens/s sustained.
- Peak target for 3–7 minute spikes (220 RPS) -> ~30,800 tokens/s.

Recommended pool composition (initial):
- Sustained pool: 6x A100-80GB (handles ~12k–14k tokens/s effective when using conservative batching and cache). That covers sustained + ~30–50% headroom for growth and background cache warmups.
- Burst buffer: 2x A100-80GB as warm spares (kept pre-initialized for fast failover / transient 2–3x spikes). Warm spares are not actively serving unless utilization across pool >70% or in a configured burst window.
- Autoscaling policy: allow scaling by 1 GPU every 60–90s with a target CPU/GPU utilization trigger at 70% sustained for 3 minutes. Max autoscale cap: +4 GPUs above baseline for the first quarter, review after telemetry.
- Prewarm & cache: maintain prefix/KV cache on at least 3 nodes; ensure cache sync/replication times are <45s. Use a rolling-warm policy during predictable traffic windows (morning ramp).

Operational SLOs / runbook snippets:
- Target P99 first-token latency: <500ms during sustained windows; P95 <350ms. We expect short tail degradation during cold scale-ups.
- If scale-up latency observed >2x baseline, automatically add an additional warm spare and alert on Prometheus rule INF_POOL_DELAY.
- Eviction policy: prefer scale-down during low usage periods by shutting down the oldest burst node first and preserve a minimum of 4 GPUs running at all times.

Cost tradeoffs (short): warm spares cost but avoid cold-start latency and session failures during aggressive bursts. If cost is the primary constraint we can use faster spin-up (cached images + preloaded weights) to reduce number of warm spares.

I attached a quick capacity_model_v1.xlsx with the token->GPU mapping and a couple of scenario sheets. If you need, we can run a 48-hour soak test with synthetic traffic to validate the autoscale curve.

Next steps: Naomi will send the networking checklist; Dev will propose a test schedule and instrumentation to validate the model. If that sounds good, we’ll provide a rough cost estimate and a procurement timeline.

Adding the network checklist and a few low-level items we see tripping deployments into unexpected tails. Attaching a small patch with recommended sysctl/tcp tuning and a topology PNG.

Network checklist (concise):
- MTU: 9000 (jumbo frames) between GPU hosts and any KV/cache nodes to reduce packet overhead for large model weight pulls. Test end-to-end MTU, not just NIC setting.
- L3/L4 QoS: prioritize control plane (API <-> runtime) traffic at higher precedence than model weight sync traffic during spin-up.
- NAT / Egress: ensure NAT pool >= #concurrent nodes * 2 to avoid ephemeral port exhaustion during rollout (we recommend +25%).
- Load balancer: use connection-aware LB (preserve client affinity for session-level KV cache hits).
- NTP: strict time sync across pool (drifts cause cache validation mismatches).
- MRU trunking and LACP: ensure you have 2x 25Gb uplinks per host for sustained throughput; single uplink leads to headroom cliffs under burst.

Tuning highlights in patch: tcp_tw_reuse, net.ipv4.tcp_fastopen, increased somaxconn, and bumping the NIC rx/tx ring sizes. We included a small patch file (network_changes.patch) with recommended values and a quick validation command list.

If Cleo’s CloudOps wants, we can run an initial network validation script from our side (takes ~90m) to check MTU, route MTU, and ephemeral port headroom.

Naomi Feldman
